summary: For 8–9 year olds learning what uses electricity at home (UK KS2 Year 4: 'identify common appliances that run on electricity'). The learning goal is a clean three-way mental sort — mains (wall socket) vs battery vs not-electric — anchored in children's own homes, plus the safety habit that mains sockets/plugs/cables are never for experimenting and only battery-powered things are safe to explore. The work is categorisation and safety awareness, not circuit theory, current, or quantities. Deliberate foils (a candle, a wind-up/clockwork toy, a gas hob) break the misconception that anything moving, noisy, or switch-on uses electricity.
misconceptions: 'Anything that moves or makes noise uses electricity' — children over-include wind-up toys, clockwork and friction-driven things; foils are needed to break this.
'Battery things aren't really electricity' — some children reserve the word for the mains; the battery torch and the wall lamp both use electricity.
'Plugging in charges it up forever' — confusion between charging a battery and being powered while plugged in; not resolved here but worth noting for later.
Treating gas appliances (gas hob, gas fire) as electrical because they are kitchen/heating devices.
Believing the socket itself is 'the electricity' rather than a supply the appliance draws from.

activities.title: Spot the electrical things in a home scene
steps: Walk through a labelled home picture (kitchen, lounge, bedroom) and name the devices you see.
Tap or point to each device and say whether it runs on electricity, and if so whether its power comes from the mains (wall socket) or from a battery.

For each device, reveal or state a short fact: e.g. toaster — 'Mains: I plug into the wall. Wall sockets are grown-up only, never poke them'; torch — 'Battery: safe for you to open and explore'; candle or wind-up clock — 'No electricity at all.'
Explain for each item how you can tell — does it have a plug and lead to a socket, or does it carry a battery inside?

Discuss the deliberate foils: a gas hob (may look electric, but its heat comes from burning gas; some use a small electric spark only to light it) and a clockwork/wind-up toy (moves but isn't mains/battery electric).
activities.insight: The sort isn't simply 'electric or not' but THREE piles — mains, battery, not-electric — and the mains pile is exactly the dangerous one you must never build with, so the only things safe to experiment with are the battery ones.

activities.title: Sort the appliances into three bins
steps: Take a set of appliance cards and place each into one of three labelled bins: Mains, Battery, Not electric.
For a wrong placement, use the hint 'does it have a plug or a battery?' and try again.

Handle edge-case cards (a phone, a car) by discussing rather than scoring: a phone has a battery AND charges from the mains; a petrol or diesel car burns fuel to move but uses a battery for its electric lights, while an electric car runs on a big battery.
Name at least ten appliances and place them, then say aloud the rule you used to sort.
activities.insight: Sorting by energy source (mains vs battery vs not-electric) is an active, self-correcting way to build and firm up the mental model, and edge cases show the piles aren't always clean-cut.

activities.title: Odd-one-out and power-source matching
steps: Given a small group of appliances, pick the odd one out (e.g. the one that does not run on electricity) and say why.
Match each device to its power source (mains socket icon vs battery/cell icon).
Answer 'which of these run on electricity?' and justify the choice by energy source, not just by appearance.
activities.insight: Quick recognition tasks let a learner check and firm up the mains/battery/not-electric sort across many examples.

activities.title: Ask the electrician: why and what's safe
steps: Pose questions to an in-role 'electrician' character, e.g. 'is the toaster electric?' or 'why can't I poke the socket?'
Ask 'where does the electricity come from?' for a mains item and for a battery item, and compare the answers.
Restate the safety rule in your own words: mains sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting; only battery-powered circuits are safe to build.
activities.insight: Talking through 'why' reinforces the safety habit and the idea that mains and battery are both electricity from different supplies.

activities.title: Two-tier check: four things, which use electricity and how?
steps: Look at four things: a torch that takes batteries, a gas cooker, a wind-up radio, and a fridge plugged into the wall.
Say which ones use electricity to work.
For the ones that do, say how you can tell which get their electricity from the mains and which from a battery.

Answer deeper probes: how can a wind-up radio with no battery and no plug still use electricity? When a phone is plugged in, is it mains or battery, and what's happening to the battery? Name three things at home that make heat — which get that heat from electricity and which from burning something? If the power cut off in your street, which of the four things would still work, and why?
activities.insight: Classifying by electrical energy source (mains vs battery vs self-generated) — rather than by 'has a plug' — is what separates a surface sort from real understanding, and extends to new cases like a power cut or a phone charging.

checkQuestion: Look at these four things: a torch that takes batteries, a gas cooker, a wind-up radio, and a fridge plugged into the wall. Which ones use electricity to work, and how can you tell which get their electricity from the mains and which from a battery?
checkAnswer: The battery torch and the mains fridge use electricity; the gas cooker burns gas, not electricity; the wind-up radio makes its own electricity from a spring you wind, so it uses electricity but needs no battery or plug. Mains appliances have a plug/lead to a wall socket; battery ones carry their energy inside a battery and have no plug.
